4.2 Viscosity: Newton's law of viscous flow, Stokes' law and terminal velocity, Poiseuille's formula
4.3 Equation of continuity and Bernoulli's principle with applications

html:
Fluids — liquids and gases — carry the blood in our arteries, the water in our pipes and the air over an aeroplane wing. Of the 10 Mechanics questions , with about 1 questions from this chapter.

It is a formula-rich chapter, so the question is usually a quick ratio: how a capillary rise, a terminal velocity or a flow rate changes when a radius changes, an excess pressure inside a bubble, or a speed or pressure from the continuity and Bernoulli equations.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • P = P_0 + h\rho g; Pascal's law and the hydraulic lift; floating and Archimedes' principle.
  • Surface tension T = F/l and surface energy (same number, J m⁻² = N m⁻¹); effect of temperature and impurities.
  • Excess pressure 2T/r in a drop or an air bubble, 4T/r in a soap bubble; work to make a film counts both surfaces.
  • Capillary rise h = 2T\cos\theta/(r\rho g): h \propto 1/r; angle of contact; mercury is depressed.
  • Viscosity: F = \eta A\,dv/dx; Stokes' law 6\pi\eta rv; terminal velocity \propto r^2; Poiseuille Q \propto r^4.
  • Continuity A_1v_1 = A_2v_2; Bernoulli P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho gh = constant; Torricelli v = \sqrt{2gh}; lift, venturi, atomiser.

4.1 Pressure in a fluid; surface tension, surface energy and capillary action

Pressure in a fluid at rest

Pressure is the normal force per unit area: P = F/A. It is a scalar; SI unit pascal (1 Pa = 1 N m⁻²), dimensions [ML^{-1}T^{-2}].

Other units: 1 atm = 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa = 76 cm of mercury = 760 torr; 1 bar = 10⁵ Pa; 1 mm Hg ≈ 133 Pa (blood pressure of 120 mm Hg is about 16 kPa above atmospheric).

In a fluid at rest:

  1. pressure at a point acts equally in all directions;
  2. pressure is the same at all points at the same level in a connected body of the same liquid;
  3. pressure increases with depth: at depth h below the free surface P = P_0 + h\rho g, where P_0 is the atmospheric pressure. h\rho g alone is the gauge pressure; P is the absolute pressure;
  4. pressure at the bottom does not depend on the shape or the cross-section of the vessel, only on the depth (the hydrostatic paradox).

The atmosphere supports a column of 76 cm of mercury, or about 10.3 m of water.

Pascal's law

A pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and to the walls of the container.

In a hydraulic lift, press or brake, a small force F_1 on a small piston A_1 gives a large force F_2 = F_1A_2/A_1 on a large piston — but the large piston moves a correspondingly smaller distance, so no work is gained.

Archimedes' principle: a body wholly or partly immersed in a fluid feels an upward buoyant force (upthrust) equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.

A floating body displaces its own weight of fluid, so the fraction of its volume submerged is \rho_{body}/\rho_{fluid} (ice, 917 kg m⁻³, floats about nine-tenths submerged in fresh water).

Relative density = weight in air / loss of weight in water.

Worked example 4.1 — a diver and a hydraulic lift

Problem.(a) Find the absolute pressure on a diver 10 m below the surface of Phewa Lake (P_0 = 1.01\times10^5 Pa, \rho = 1000 kg m⁻³, g = 9.8 m s⁻²).(b) The pistons of a car-service lift have areas 10 cm² and 1000 cm². What force on the small piston lifts a 2000 kg car?

Solution.(a) P = 1.01\times10^5 + 1000(9.8)(10) = 1.99\times10^5 Pa — about 2 atm: every 10 m of water adds roughly one atmosphere.(b) F_1 = F_2A_1/A_2 = 2000(9.8)/100 = 196 N.

Surface tension

Molecules attract one another over a very short molecular range (about 10⁻⁹ m). A molecule deep in a liquid is pulled equally on all sides; a molecule in the surface is pulled inward only.

The surface therefore behaves like a stretched elastic membrane and tends to contract to the least area — which is why free drops and bubbles are spherical (a sphere has the least surface for a given volume), why a greased needle can float on water, and why wet hairs of a paint brush cling together.

Attraction between like molecules is cohesion; between unlike molecules (liquid and solid), adhesion.

Surface tension

The surface tension T of a liquid is the force per unit length acting on an imaginary line drawn in the liquid surface, perpendicular to the line and tangential to the surface: T = F/l. SI unit N m⁻¹; dimensions [MT^{-2}].

Surface energy. To increase the area of a surface, molecules must be brought up from the interior against the inward pull, so work is needed.

The work done per unit increase in surface area (at constant temperature) is the surface energy, and it is numerically equal to the surface tension: W = T\,\Delta A (1 J m⁻² = 1 N m⁻¹).

Situation Change of area to use in W = T\Delta A
Liquid drop of radius r (one surface) 4\pi r^2
Soap bubble of radius r (two surfaces, inside and outside) 2\times4\pi r^2 = 8\pi r^2
Soap film on a frame, area increased by \Delta A 2\Delta A
Drop of radius R split into n equal droplets 4\pi R^2(n^{1/3} - 1) — energy must be supplied

When small drops merge into one big drop the total area falls and energy is released (the big drop is slightly warmer).

Excess pressure inside a curved surface (the inside of the curve is at the higher pressure):

Surface Excess pressure
Liquid drop, or air bubble inside a liquid (one surface) \Delta P = \frac{2T}{r}
Soap bubble in air (two surfaces) \Delta P = \frac{4T}{r}

The smaller the bubble, the larger the excess pressure. Two soap bubbles of different sizes joined by a tube: air flows from the smaller into the larger, so the small one shrinks and the large one grows.

What changes surface tension.

Factor Effect on T
Rise in temperature decreases (almost linearly); zero at the critical temperature
Highly soluble impurity (common salt in water) increases slightly
Sparingly soluble or surface-active impurity (soap, detergent, phenol) decreases strongly
Oil or grease film on water decreases (oil spread on ponds kills mosquito larvae, which can no longer hang from the surface)

Detergents lower the surface tension of water so that it spreads into and wets the fine gaps of cloth; hot soapy water washes better than cold, plain water.

Angle of contact and capillary action

Angle of contact

The angle of contact is the angle between the tangent to the liquid surface at the point of contact and the solid surface, measured inside the liquid.

Pure water and clean glass Mercury and glass
Angle of contact acute, nearly 0° (often quoted as about 8°) obtuse, about 140°
Adhesion vs cohesion adhesion > cohesion cohesion > adhesion
Wets the glass? yes no
Meniscus concave (curves up at the walls) convex (curves down at the walls)
In a capillary tube rises is depressed

At exactly 90° (water on silver) there is neither rise nor fall.

Capillarity is the rise or fall of a liquid in a tube of very fine bore. Balancing the upward surface-tension pull around the rim, 2\pi rT\cos\theta, against the weight of the raised column, \pi r^2h\rho g (Jurin's law):

h = \frac{2T\cos\theta}{r\rho g}

So h \propto 1/r (hr = constant for a given liquid): halve the bore and the liquid rises twice as high. For \theta > 90^{\circ}, \cos\theta < 0 and h is negative (depression).

Applications. Oil rises in a lamp wick; ink in blotting paper; water in a towel and in the soil (ploughing breaks the fine soil capillaries and keeps moisture from reaching the surface and evaporating); surface tension and capillarity help move water in the xylem of plants.

A capillary tube never overflows

If the tube above the water is shorter than h, the water rises to the top and stops — it does not spill over like a fountain. The meniscus flattens instead: its radius of curvature R grows so that hR stays constant.

In a freely falling lift (g_{eff} = 0) water rises to fill the whole length of any capillary.

Worked example 4.2 — capillary rise and bubbles

Problem.(a) Water (T = 0.07 N m⁻¹, \theta = 0^{\circ}) stands in a glass capillary of internal diameter 0.5 mm. Find the rise (g = 9.8 m s⁻²).(b) Find the excess pressure inside a soap bubble of radius 2 cm, and the work done in blowing a bubble of radius 1 cm, for a soap solution with T = 0.03 N m⁻¹.

Solution.(a) r = 0.25 mm: h = \frac{2(0.07)}{(0.25\times10^{-3})(1000)(9.8)} = 0.057 m = 5.7 cm.(b) \Delta P = 4T/r = 4(0.03)/0.02 = 6 Pa. Work = T\times8\pi r^2 = 0.03\times8\pi\times10^{-4} = 7.5\times10^{-5} J.

4.2 Viscosity: Newton's law of viscous flow, Stokes' law and terminal velocity, Poiseuille's formula

Viscosity and Newton's law

In streamline (laminar) flow a liquid moves in layers that slide over one another: the layer touching a fixed surface is at rest, and the speed increases layer by layer away from it.

Viscosity is the property of a fluid by which it opposes the relative motion between its adjacent layers — internal friction of the fluid.

Newton's law of viscous flow

The tangential viscous force between two layers is proportional to the area A of the layers and to the velocity gradient dv/dx (rate of change of velocity with distance perpendicular to the flow): F = \eta A\frac{dv}{dx}.

The constant \eta is the coefficient of viscosity. SI unit N s m⁻² = Pa s (sometimes called the decapoise); CGS unit the poise; 1 Pa s = 10 poise. Dimensions [ML^{-1}T^{-1}].

Liquids Gases
Origin of viscosity cohesive forces between molecules transfer of momentum by molecules moving between layers
On heating viscosity decreases (honey and engine oil run more freely) viscosity increases

Viscosity is different from density: honey is far more viscous than mercury, though much less dense. Blood is about three to four times as viscous as water.

Reynolds number R_e = \rho vD/\eta (dimensionless) decides the type of flow in a pipe of diameter D: small values (below about 2000) mean laminar flow, large values turbulent flow.

The speed at which laminar flow breaks down is the critical velocity v_c = R_e\eta/(\rho D) — high for thick, viscous liquids in narrow tubes.

Stokes' law and terminal velocity

Stokes' law

A small sphere of radius r moving slowly with speed v through a viscous fluid of viscosity \eta feels a viscous drag F = 6\pi\eta rv.

It holds for a small, smooth, rigid sphere, moving slowly (streamline flow) through a uniform fluid of large extent. Dimensional check: [ML^{-1}T^{-1}][L][LT^{-1}] = [MLT^{-2}].

A sphere of density \rho dropped in a fluid of density \sigma accelerates until the drag plus the upthrust balance its weight. Then it falls at a constant terminal velocity:

\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\rho g = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\sigma g + 6\pi\eta rv_t \quad\Rightarrow\quad v_t = \frac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}

  • v_t \propto r^2: double the radius, four times the terminal velocity.
  • If \sigma > \rho (an air bubble in water), v_t is negative: the body rises at a steady speed.
  • Tiny water droplets in clouds and fog have very small v_t, so they seem to float; a parachute has a small terminal velocity because its drag is large.
  • Uses: Millikan's oil-drop experiment (Chapter 18); measuring the viscosity of oils; settling (sedimentation) of particles. In medicine, the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is the rate at which red cells settle in a column of blood — clumped cells behave as larger spheres and settle faster.

Worked example 4.3 — why clouds float

Problem. Find the terminal velocity of a cloud droplet of radius 10 μm falling through air (\eta = 1.8\times10^{-5} Pa s, density of water 1000 kg m⁻³; neglect the density of air; g = 9.8 m s⁻²). How fast would a droplet of radius 30 μm fall?

Solution. v_t = \frac{2(10^{-5})^2(1000)(9.8)}{9(1.8\times10^{-5})} = 1.2\times10^{-2} m s⁻¹ — about 1 cm per second, so air currents easily hold it up. Three times the radius gives 3^2 = 9 times the speed: about 11 cm s⁻¹.

Poiseuille's formula

For steady laminar flow of a liquid through a narrow horizontal tube of radius r and length l, with a pressure difference P between its ends, the volume of liquid flowing per second is

Q = \frac{\pi Pr^4}{8\eta l}

The formula can be checked (apart from the \pi/8) by dimensions. The key is the fourth power of the radius: halve the radius and the flow drops to \frac{1}{16}.

Writing Q = P/R, the tube has a fluid resistance R = \frac{8\eta l}{\pi r^4}; tubes in series add resistances and tubes in parallel add flows, exactly like electrical resistors.

Worked example 4.4 — a narrowed artery

Problem. Fatty deposits reduce the radius of an artery by 20 %. For the same pressure difference, by what factor does the blood flow fall? By what factor must the pressure difference rise to restore the flow?

Solution. Q \propto r^4: 0.8^4 = 0.41, so the flow falls to 41 % of normal. To restore it, P must rise by 1/0.41 \approx 2.4 times — one reason narrowed arteries raise blood pressure and load the heart.

4.3 Equation of continuity and Bernoulli's principle with applications

An ideal fluid is incompressible and non-viscous, and its flow is steady and irrotational.

In steady (streamline) flow the velocity at each point does not change with time; the path of a fluid particle is a streamline, the tangent to it gives the velocity there, and two streamlines never cross. Crowded streamlines mean fast flow.

Equation of continuity

For an incompressible fluid flowing steadily through a tube, the mass (and volume) entering one end per second equals that leaving the other:

A_1v_1 = A_2v_2 = Q \ \ \text{(constant)}

Q is the volume flow rate (m³ s⁻¹). Where the tube is narrow, the flow is fast: water speeds up through the rapids of a gorge and out of a nozzle; a thumb over the end of a hose makes the jet fly farther.

It is the law of conservation of mass. In the body, the total cross-section of all the capillaries is far larger than that of the aorta, so blood moves much more slowly in the capillaries — giving time for exchange with the tissues.

Bernoulli's principle

Bernoulli's theorem

For the steady flow of an ideal fluid, the sum of the pressure, the kinetic energy per unit volume and the potential energy per unit volume is the same at every point of a streamline: P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho gh = constant.

Dividing by \rho g: \frac{P}{\rho g} + \frac{v^2}{2g} + h = constant — the sum of the pressure head, velocity head and gravitational head. Bernoulli's theorem is the law of conservation of energy for a moving fluid.

In a horizontal pipe it says: where the speed is high, the pressure is low.

Applications.

Device or effect How Bernoulli and continuity explain it
Venturimeter the pressure drop between the wide part and the throat gives the flow speed: P_1 - P_2 = \frac{1}{2}\rho(v_2^2 - v_1^2) with A_1v_1 = A_2v_2
Torricelli's theorem liquid leaves a hole at depth h below the free surface of a wide open tank with speed v = \sqrt{2gh} — the speed of a free fall from that height
Lift on an aeroplane wing (aerofoil) air flows faster over the curved upper surface, so the pressure above is lower than below
Roofs lifted off in a storm fast wind over the roof lowers the pressure above it; the still air inside pushes up
Two boats or trains moving side by side fast flow in the narrow gap lowers the pressure there; they are pushed together
Atomiser, sprayer, Bunsen burner, carburettor a fast jet past the top of a tube lowers the pressure there and draws the liquid (or air) in
Swing of a spinning ball (Magnus effect) the spin makes the air faster on one side; the ball is pushed toward the low-pressure side

Jet from a hole: for a tank filled to height H with a hole at depth h below the surface, the jet lands at a horizontal distance R = 2\sqrt{h(H - h)} from the foot of the tank — greatest (R = H) for a hole halfway down, and the same for holes at depths h and H - h.

Worked example 4.5 — venturi and Torricelli

Problem.(a) Water flows through a horizontal pipe whose cross-section narrows from 4 cm² to 1 cm². The speed in the wide part is 1 m s⁻¹. Find the speed in the narrow part and the pressure difference.(b) Water stands 5 m above a small hole in the side of a large open tank. Find the speed of efflux (g = 10 m s⁻²).

Solution.(a) v_2 = A_1v_1/A_2 = 4 m s⁻¹; P_1 - P_2 = \frac{1}{2}(1000)(4^2 - 1^2) = 7500 Pa (a water column of about 0.77 m).(b) v = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{100} = 10 m s⁻¹.

Continuity uses area, area uses the square of the diameter

A pipe narrowing from 4 cm to 2 cm diameter has one quarter of the area, so the speed becomes four times, not two. And in Bernoulli's equation use v^2: doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic-energy term.

Ratio problems in this chapter

Learn the power of r in each formula and most questions are one line: capillary rise h \propto r^{-1}; excess pressure \propto r^{-1}; Stokes' drag \propto r; terminal velocity \propto r^2; Poiseuille flow \propto r^4; speed in a pipe \propto r^{-2} (continuity).

Formula and fact sheet

Stokes' law F = 6\pi\eta rv
Terminal velocity v_t = 2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g/9\eta; \propto r^2
Poiseuille Q = \pi Pr^4/(8\eta l); \propto r^4; resistance 8\eta l/\pi r^4
Reynolds number R_e = \rho vD/\eta; low → laminar, high → turbulent
Continuity A_1v_1 = A_2v_2 (mass conservation)
Bernoulli P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho gh = constant (energy conservation)

Chapter summary

  • Pressure in a liquid is P_0 + h\rho g, the same at one level, independent of the vessel's shape; Pascal's law multiplies force in a hydraulic lift; upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced.
  • Surface tension (N m⁻¹) equals surface energy per unit area (J m⁻²); it falls with temperature and with soap or detergent; a soap film has two surfaces.
  • Excess pressure is 2T/r in a drop and 4T/r in a soap bubble — the smaller the bubble, the higher the pressure.
  • Capillary rise h = 2T\cos\theta/(r\rho g): liquids that wet glass (acute angle, concave meniscus) rise; mercury (obtuse, convex) is depressed; a short tube never overflows.
  • Viscous force F = \eta A\,dv/dx; viscosity of liquids falls and of gases rises on heating; SI unit Pa s.
  • Stokes' drag 6\pi\eta rv leads to the terminal velocity 2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g/9\eta, proportional to r^2.
  • Poiseuille's flow Q = \pi Pr^4/8\eta l depends on the fourth power of the radius.
  • Continuity A_1v_1 = A_2v_2 and Bernoulli P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho gh = constant: faster flow means lower pressure — venturimeter, Torricelli's \sqrt{2gh}, wing lift, atomisers.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (b) — pressure is force per unit area: 1 Pa = 1 N m⁻². N m⁻¹ is the unit of surface tension.

2. (c) — the atmosphere presses on the surface and the liquid column adds h\rho g; h\rho g alone is the gauge pressure.

3. (d) — the pressure applied at the small piston is transmitted undiminished to the large one, so F_2 = F_1A_2/A_1.

4. (a) — T = F/l: [MLT^{-2}]/[L] = [MT^{-2}]. (c) is pressure.

5. (b) — surface tension falls (almost linearly) with temperature and vanishes at the critical temperature.

6. (c) — a soap bubble has two surfaces, so the excess pressure is 2\times2T/r = 4T/r. 2T/r is for a drop or an air bubble inside a liquid.

7. (d) — about 140°: mercury does not wet glass, its meniscus is convex and it is depressed in a capillary.

8. (a) — with \theta < 90^{\circ}, \cos\theta > 0 and h = 2T\cos\theta/(r\rho g) is positive.

9. (d) — Jurin's law: h = 2T\cos\theta/(r\rho g), so hr is constant.

10. (b) — \eta = F/(A\,dv/dx) has unit N s m⁻² = Pa s. The poise is the CGS unit (1 Pa s = 10 poise).

11. (a) — Stokes' law, F = 6\pi\eta rv, valid for small spheres in slow (streamline) motion.

12. (c) — v_t = 2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g/9\eta: weight and upthrust go as r^3, drag as rv, so v \propto r^2.

13. (a) — Q = \pi Pr^4/(8\eta l); the fourth power is the point examiners test.

14. (b) — gas viscosity comes from molecules carrying momentum between layers; faster molecules at higher temperature carry more. Liquids behave oppositely.

15. (c) — what enters a tube per second must leave it: \rho A_1v_1 = \rho A_2v_2.

16. (a) — P, \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 and \rho gh are energies per unit volume; their sum stays constant.

17. (d) — Torricelli's theorem: the efflux speed equals the speed of free fall through the height h.

18. (b) — the pressure difference between its wide part and its throat gives the flow speed and hence the rate of flow.

19. (b) — surface energy (J m⁻²) and surface tension (N m⁻¹) have the same dimensions and the same numerical value.

20. (c) — \eta = F/(A\,dv/dx): [MLT^{-2}]/([L^2][T^{-1}]) = [ML^{-1}T^{-1}].

21. (d) — surface tension makes the surface contract to the least area, and a sphere has the least area for its volume.

Answers and explanations — Set B

1. (b) — a capillary never overflows; the water stops at the top and the meniscus radius grows (hR constant), so the meniscus becomes flatter.

2. (d) — in free fall the effective g is zero, so nothing pulls the column down: h = 2T\cos\theta/(r\rho g) grows without limit and the water fills the tube.

3. (a) — excess pressure 4T/r is greater in the smaller bubble, so air is pushed into the larger one; the small bubble shrinks further.

4. (c) — h \propto 1/r: half the radius gives twice the rise.

Model answer D1: Bernoulli's theorem and its applications (10 marks)

Introduction. For the steady, streamline flow of an ideal fluid (incompressible and non-viscous), the equation of continuity A_1v_1 = A_2v_2 expresses conservation of mass. Bernoulli's theorem expresses conservation of energy.

Statement. For the streamline flow of an ideal fluid, the sum of the pressure energy, kinetic energy and potential energy per unit volume is constant at every point: P + \tfrac12\rho v^2 + \rho gh = \text{constant}.

Derivation. A fluid flows through a pipe from section 1 (area A_1, pressure P_1, height h_1) to section 2. In time \Delta t a volume V passes each section. The net work done by pressure is (P_1 - P_2)V.

The gain in kinetic energy is \tfrac12\rho V(v_2^2 - v_1^2) and the gain in potential energy is \rho Vg(h_2 - h_1). By the work-energy theorem, (P_1 - P_2)V = \tfrac12\rho V(v_2^2 - v_1^2) + \rho Vg(h_2 - h_1).

Dividing by V and rearranging gives P_1 + \tfrac12\rho v_1^2 + \rho gh_1 = P_2 + \tfrac12\rho v_2^2 + \rho gh_2.

Applications.

  1. Venturi meter. It measures flow rate from the pressure drop at the narrow throat.
  2. Aerofoil (wing). Faster air on top means lower pressure, so there is a net upward lift.
  3. Atomiser and spray gun. Fast air over a tube lowers the pressure and pushes the liquid up.
  4. Speed of efflux (Torricelli). v = \sqrt{2gh} for a hole at depth h.
  5. Blowing off a roof. Fast wind over the roof lowers the outside pressure and the inside air pushes the roof up.
  6. Bunsen burner and carburettor draw in air or fuel by the same low-pressure effect.
Quantity Meaning
P static pressure energy per unit volume
\tfrac12\rho v^2 kinetic energy per unit volume
\rho gh potential energy per unit volume

Numerical. Water (\rho = 1000\ \text{kg m}^{-3}) flows at 2\ \text{m s}^{-1} in a horizontal pipe of cross-section 40\ \text{cm}^2, which narrows to 10\ \text{cm}^2. Continuity gives v_2 = 2\times40/10 = 8\ \text{m s}^{-1}.

Then P_1 - P_2 = \tfrac12(1000)(64 - 4) = 3.0\times10^4\ \text{Pa}.

Conclusion. Where a fluid moves faster, its pressure is lower. This one idea explains lift, sprays and flow meters.

Model answer D2: viscosity, Stokes' law and terminal velocity (10 marks)

Introduction. Viscosity is the internal friction of a fluid that opposes the relative motion between its layers.

Newton's law gives the viscous force F = \eta A\dfrac{dv}{dx}, where \eta is the coefficient of viscosity with SI unit pascal second (Pa s) and dimensions [ML^{-1}T^{-1}].

Stokes' law. A small sphere of radius r moving at speed v through a fluid of viscosity \eta meets a viscous drag F = 6\pi\eta rv.

Terminal velocity. A sphere of density \rho falls in a liquid of density \sigma. Three forces act on it:

  1. weight W = \tfrac43\pi r^3\rho g downward;
  2. upthrust U = \tfrac43\pi r^3\sigma g upward;
  3. viscous drag 6\pi\eta rv upward, which grows with speed.

At terminal velocity the net force is zero: \tfrac43\pi r^3(\rho - \sigma)g = 6\pi\eta rv_t, so

v_t = \frac{2r^2(\rho - \sigma)g}{9\eta}

The terminal velocity is proportional to r^2, so a large drop falls faster than a small one. A bubble or a lighter object (\rho < \sigma) rises with a negative v_t.

Point Liquid Gas
Viscosity with temperature Decreases when heated Increases when heated
Reason Weaker molecular attraction More molecular collisions
Example Hot oil flows easily Hot air is more viscous

Uses. Stokes' law explains why raindrops reach a steady speed, why clouds float and how Millikan measured the electron charge. It is also the basis of the falling-ball viscometer.

Numerical. A steel ball of radius 1\ \text{mm} and density 7800\ \text{kg m}^{-3} falls in glycerine (\sigma = 1260\ \text{kg m}^{-3}, \eta = 0.83\ \text{Pa s}).

Then v_t = \dfrac{2(10^{-3})^2(7800 - 1260)(9.8)}{9(0.83)} = 1.7\times10^{-2}\ \text{m s}^{-1}, that is about 1.7\ \text{cm s}^{-1}.

Conclusion. The ball speeds up until drag plus upthrust equals the weight, and it then falls at the constant terminal velocity v_t.
